title: Are You My Mother?: How Animal Imprinting Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore animal imprinting, focusing on precocial birds such as ducks and geese. They cover ancient and rural Chinese duck-herding uses of imprinting, Konrad Lorenz's discovery and coining of filial imprinting and the critical period, his Nazi-era affiliation and the criticism that followed, and Oscar Heinroth's earlier work with graylag geese. They then describe Eckhard Hess and Ao Ramsey's refinement of the critical period in mallard ducklings, sexual imprinting in birds (including jackdaws), and Joe Hutto's turkey work. The episode moves to mammals: Harry Harlow's monkey experiments and their role in the animal rights movement, Keith Kendrick's sheep-and-goat switching study, and Harlow's finding that comfort and contact, not food, drive attachment. It closes with applications in wildlife conservation (Operation Condor, ultralight aircraft, panda handling) and a listener mail recommendation of the book Gang Leader for a Day.

segments.title: Opening banter and imprinting introduction
segments.summary: The hosts joke around, debate pronunciation of imprinting, and introduce animal imprinting as a process mainly seen in precocial birds that form attachments to a parent figure, which need not be biological or even alive.

segments.title: Historical and folk uses of imprinting
segments.summary: A Roman treatise advised raising wild duck eggs under domestic hens, and rural Chinese rice farmers imprinted ducklings on a stick to lead them to fields to eat snails. The hosts note ducklings imprint within a few hours of hatching.

segments.title: Nature versus nurture in imprinting
segments.summary: The hosts frame imprinting as a natural experiment in nature versus nurture: precocial ducks are hardwired to seek attachment, but the environment determines the object attached to.

segments.title: Konrad Lorenz and his Nazi affiliation
segments.summary: Konrad Lorenz, an Austrian zoologist, earned a PhD in 1933 and was a founder of ethology. He was criticized for enthusiastically welcoming the Nazis and applying racial theory, and for denying party membership until proven otherwise. Science has partly forgiven him, though some scientists still object. He was also accused of extrapolating animal findings to humans.

segments.title: Oscar Heinroth's early work and Lorenz's experiments
segments.summary: Oscar Heinroth first studied graylag geese imprinting without using the term. Lorenz separated goslings from their mothers, then showed they followed him when a box was lifted. He coined filial imprinting and proposed a critical period of roughly the first hour and irreversibility.

segments.title: Hess and Ramsey refine the critical period
segments.summary: Later studies by Eckhard Hess and Ao Ramsey in Maryland used mallard ducklings and found the most sensitive period was 13 to 16 hours after hatching. Ducklings that worked harder to reach the parent bonded more strongly. Ducklings also imprinted on colored paper-mache decoys, with color, smell, and touch as cues.

segments.title: Turkey imprinting and sexual imprinting in birds
segments.summary: Joe Hutto's turkey work, shown in the PBS Nature special My Life as a Turkey, is discussed, including talking turkey to eggs before hatching. Birds also imprint sexually, which can lead them to prefer humans or other species as mates, but they are sexually blind to their raising parent. Jackdaw studies suggested different sensitive periods for filial and sexual imprinting.

segments.title: Imprinting in mammals and Harry Harlow's monkeys
segments.summary: Harry Harlow's monkey experiments are described, including the wire and terry-cloth surrogate mothers. Monkeys preferred the cloth mother even when fed by the wire one, showing comfort and contact matter more than food. Harlow's work fueled the animal rights movement, and he was famously quoted as saying 'who could ever love a monkey?'

segments.title: Sheep-goat switch study and mammal attachment
segments.summary: Keith Kendrick's 1990s study swapped sheep and goats at birth. Females later reverted to their own species after being returned, while males kept a preference for the species that raised them. The hosts note oxytocin release during skin-to-skin contact as relevant to bonding.

segments.title: Applications in conservation and cross-species adoption
segments.summary: Wildlife conservationists now avoid human contact: Operation Condor raised abandoned condor chicks with a puppet dressed as a condor and used ultralight planes to teach migration. Pandas handled too young by humans fared poorly. Socialization matters, and inanimate-mother monkeys often became inadequate mothers. The hosts mention cross-species adoptions, such as a lioness raising antelope calves.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to related episodes and the search bar, then close the show.

segments.title: Listener mail: gang book recommendation
segments.summary: A listener recommends Sudhir Venkatesh's Gang Leader for a Day, a sociological account of befriending a Chicago gang leader, and a New York Times article about it. The hosts close with requests for feedback.
